EMERGENCY CALLS

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Emergency 10111! With 7 million dropped calls, SA’s most important number isn’t doing its job. Just how dysfunctional are the call centres and how devastating are the effects down the line?

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa’s most dialed emergency number SAPS’s 10111 is only operating at 40% capacity. Provincial call centres are understaffed, the employees overworked, underpaid and in some cases working in squalid conditions under tough working practices. We get the inside track from two 10111 operators – one in Gauteng, the other in Durban – exposing the root causes of SA’s crisis in emergency service delivery. And what of the callers in distress, for whom this crisis is a matter of life and death? Where do victims of crime, rape and distress turn to when there is no one on the other end of the line? Even if the calls were answered timeously and efficiently what capacity does the Police Service have to respond to the emergency? Through personal stories and an inside look into how an efficient call centre works, we lay bare the flaws in the police value chain and the impact it has on South Africans who are in desperate need of protection living in one of the most violent and dangerous countries in the world.

Summary:
If you call 10111 in an emergency the likelihood is you won’t get the assistance you need in the timeframe you require it, or you may not be assisted at all. These are the findings from a parliamentary question answered by Police Minister Bheki Cele.

I have tracked down two whistleblowers who are prepared to expose their working hell. Both wish to hide their identity but we can get footage of their working environments, one in Durban, the other in midrand – and they will tell their side of the real story behind the devastating government statistics which prove the failure 10111 is, for South Africans when they’re in urgent need of help.

Anastasia will never know if her husband’s life might have been saved if there was someone on the other end of the line. Katlego has lost faith in the police, because even though her call was answered by 10111 after being strangled by her brother, when a vehicle was dispatched to help her she was neglected and mistreated by the police, no emergency vehicle was even sent to get her to a hospital. Ash was facing a drunk, aggressive and violent boyfriend when she frantically called 10111. After no response she called the local police station. Luckily they answered but what happened next, makes the response call almost laughable.

We speak to people who have become casualties of the 10111 crisis and look at how, even if the number was working at full efficiency, policing down the line may be inadequate to deal with responses effectively. We get an inside look into how an optimal call centre should operate and what is needed to get the assistance required by victims of crime or medical emergency. So the call by the Minister of Police for more recruits to man the centres may not be a solution. Is there a private public partnership and technology that can be a game changer to protecting lives? But at what cost and who will foot the bill in the end?

Further information:
On 3rd January 2023, in response to a parliamentary question by DA Shadow Minister of Police Andrew Whitfield, the following shocking statistics were revealed by Minister of Police Bheki Cele:

Only about 40% of required call centre staff were employed across SA.
The 10111 number requires police response and more than 7 million calls were dropped. Only 40% of calls were answered. Three provinces. Limpopo, Free State and Northern Cape were unable to give any feedback for the period requested - 2020/21 and 2021/22 to present.

The crisis is so severe, that during December when it was required for 126 staff to be working, there were only 12. Many staff members were absent and unable to attend work as they were overworked and could not handle the pressure, according to Claude Naicker, National Manager PSA.

The PSA have requested an urgent turnaround plan from Gen. Fani Masimola, within 30 days. But already there is misleading information from the Ministry of Police saying that they have recruited 10 000 new members, but none of these are destined for the call centres according to Naicker, and furthermore, the staff manning the lines has to be trained to be able to deal with the emergencies. This week the Ministry announced they were recruiting more people to man the centres. The question is, is there police capacity to respond on the ground and how long will it take to train and get these members trained and up to speed?

In our story on Grade 4 Rape Education, we witnessed first-hand how the 10111 number remained unanswered despite a number of attempts and how the call was dropped.

The problem with the emergency number of 10111 goes much deeper. The DA have done further research and randomly called police stations directly and the results were horrific. They are willing to share that report with me.

Bobby Stevenson, Shadow MEC for Community Safety highlighted one of the most affected areas, Nelson Mandela Bay. And if one were to use it as a case study for what happens in the police value chain, from call to response, we are made even more acutely aware that South Africans are left unprotected.

In his report on the 24th of October 2022, Stevenson highlights the following.

In the Nelson Mandela Bay area, absenteeism, severe staff shortages and load shedding had damaged the area’s call centre infrastructure and crippled the call centre. The failure to answer calls is potentially life-threatening.

In response to his parliamentary question MEC Xolile Nqatha revealed that even though they had 24 lines only 2 or 3 were operational. Because of load shedding it’s taking up to 45 minutes for the phone lines to come back on. Load shedding destroyed the UPS in September which will cost R4 million to replace, so now the Command and Control Centre System is off line which means that complaints have to be taken manually with no reference numbers.

Our two case studies who work in the call centres will reveal recent conditions and confirm the under equipped environments and under staffing they experience. In Durban we will get cell phone footage and in Gauteng I aim to get undercover footage myself, in co-operation with our sources.

The frightening thing about all of this, is that even if the call centres were operating optimally could the police respond effectively to those emergencies? MEC Nqatha said that if stations have only two vehicles to attend to an emergency, they can’t proceed to the next emergency until they have completed their investigation, and some stations only have one vehicle.

So what does this all mean for the safety and security of South Africans? Who can we rely on in an emergency? And what happens to the people who are in rural areas when there isn’t even someone at the end of a line? Those people are left defenseless. But even in the heart of an urban environment citizens are left to fend for themselves.

In October 2020, Anastasia Golfinopoulou saw her husband for the last time alive, as he decided to go for a walk to the local petrol station in the northern suburbs. She decided to pack the kids in the car and go and pick him up. As she was driving down the road a car swerved in front of her and drove up the pavement. Next thing she realises it has hit someone. She jumps out the car with the driver of the vehicle that swerved and sees that he has driven over her husband who was walking home. His almost lifeless body bleeding onto the pavement. Shocked and panicked she starts calling 10111 repeatedly with no response. The other driver does the same. She even calls ER24 still no response. Finally she calls her sister who rushes over to the accident. Forty minutes go by and no one comes. They make the difficult decision to lift him off the ground and get him to a hospital. When they get to Fourways Life, he is pronounced dead a few minutes later. Anastasia has screen shots of her unanswered call logs. Even her sister tried and did not get through. Two years later she still doesn’t know who the driver of the vehicle was and the police say that her file was mixed up with someone elses. When she asks for the investigating officer she is told that he is no longer there. Anastasia is prepared to wear spy glasses and go into the police station to ask for the follow up on her case. This speaks to a system that is not even equipped to follow up on a possible culpable homicide case, let alone respond to an emergency.

One week ago Katlego was at her home in Katlehong when her brother became violent because she refused to give him the car keys. He strangled her for a very long time, to the point that she thought she was going to die. When she was able to free herself she called 10111. After a minute they answered, and said they would dispatch a vehicle, she told them she was unable to breath and that she had been strangled. They did not offer her any medical response. About 5 minutes later the police dispatch called her, and asked her if the perpetrator was still with her, she said he had left. They promptly told her to call them back when he returned, they too did not offer to get her any medical assistance. Katlego eventually got hold of her sister who rushed her to the hospital. There the doctor said she was badly strangled and that she should open a J88. When she went with her medical report to the police station to do so, she was intimidated by the police, who told her, her brother had also opened up a case of assault on her and if she continued to press charges, they would arrest her too. (She suspects that the police were friends of her 24 year old brother).

Ash was being attacked by her drunk and violent boyfriend. After numerous attempts to call 10111, she called her local police station in Douglasdale where the police did answer her call and sent a vehicle over. Initially they were very helpful and said they had to remove him from the premises. Drunk as he was they allowed him to get into his vehicle and followed him to his parents house, where he said he could stay. His parents refused to let him into the property, by which time the police had left. He then drove drunk back to Ash’s apartment, where reluctantly she had to spend a fearful night with him around.

Ash was lucky that the police station did answer their phone. In the DA’s research they randomly called 276 police stations from around the country out of 1200 police stations. Only around 40% of the police stations answered their phones. (Data to be confirmed, as I haven’t received the research yet).

In order to illustrate what a prompt response should be and what types of technology the police should be using to assist in effective 10111 calls, we have been given access to the ADT call centres. ADT with a bunch of security companies are part of the safe city initiative which is a public private partnership and helps the SAPS. They can give us access to emergency calls and how they were handled effectively. We can also follow them on a response. They can give us footage of effective apprehensions.

Wahl Baartman CEO of ADT is willing to be interviewed and speak on what an emergency call should comprise and how Private companies can assist to fill the gap in policing.

I will request a response from the Police Ministry.

7 pm - Sandton, Gauteng)

(screenshots of her phone)

Anastasia: if you saw the screenshots on my phone it was on 1% - it was dying.

VO: //( beat // But on this Sunday evening, she would join millions of people who've been let down by this critical police service.
//( beat //

(put on screen Twitter: @SAPoliceService)

VO: The Minister may always be up for good PR, but in January he was forced to admit to Parliament that 10111 command centres countrywide were only 40% staffed. Well over six million calls were dropped over three years in 6 out of 9 provinces that actually provided data, so the number is arguably more than 7 million.

Claude: How many of the 7 million calls could be people,` the most vulnerable in our society that needs assistance, that could be involved in an accident that could save somebody's life?

VO: The Public Servants Association National Manager is Claude Naicker. He’s seen the crisis escalate since a 2016 strike by its union members employed at 10111 - demanding better pay and working conditions.

Claude: Currently, if you look at Gauteng, we are operating at 74 employees. So what happens to 74 employees that have to man these voluminous calls, they eventually get burned out. During December, which is a peak period. On one shift, there were only 12 employees manning these calls

VO: The backlog becomes impossible to manage and the casualties are those whose calls go unanswered.

distant ringing tone

Anastasia: And just no one was coming.

John: So most of the calls are repeated calls for people who are not being attended to.

VO: In fear of losing his job, John confesses that it's impossible for the scant staff complement of 11 or so people, to handle up toten thousand calls a day.//
And what's worse is that some of the radio workstations are broken - a picture of systemic negligence.

John: The call taker will take your complaint to the call dispatcher. But now, when the dispatcher calls the vehicle, there are no vehicles in the area .//The reason the policemen on the ground are overwhelmed is because there are no cars to cover their area.

Katlego: He takes his arm and he starts choking me.//

VO: We wanted answers - and National Police spokesperson Brigadier Athlenda Mathe was more optimistic than her Minister.

Derek: What has led to the 10111 crisis?
Brig. Mathe: There is no crisis at all, at our 10111 call centres, we are dealing with day-to-day challenges that we are facing.

VO: Then I got the official line:
Budget has been made available to fix things.
A portion of ten thousand new recruits will alleviate staff shortages.
Roadshows have been held to assess challenges.

VO: But if we thought Gauteng was under pressure, the Durban 10111 centre is no better, judging by this footage leaked to us. This is a dramatisation of an actual conversation to protect the informant's identity"

Kate: We've got carpet that is worn, we've got cockroaches, we've got broken chairs. We've got air conditioners, that's not working. We've got only one toilet for about 70 females

Kate: our equipment here is extremely faulty it breaks all the time, all the lines are not working
Derek: Kate, what about your call monitoring screen - is that up and running?
Kate: it's not working because there's a cable that needs to be replaced and the state don't have money to replace the cable.

VO: Without this essential piece of equipment supervisors can't monitor the number of incoming calls and waiting time, leaving them unaware of the backlog.

Claude: We interviewed members, they had to at a certain stage borrow headsets from one another, share the screens in order to do their function.

VO: Hearing it from the actual 10111 staff, it was hard to accept the Brigadier's assurances - that all systems are operational and there are enough vehicles on the ground.

Derek: But we've seen the conditions Brigadier, at centres like Durban?
Brig. Mathe: all the challenges that we have experienced at the 10111 call centre in Durban are being addressed.
Mathe: We've got sufficient members in each shift to ensure that we respond to the call of duty.

VO: Our Durban whistleblower disagrees.

Kate: The equipment is broken, the telephones, you can't hear the complainants properly some phones only work off speaker.

Derek: How many operators have you got working, how many should there be?
Kate: At the moment, we have anywhere between four to seven we should have about 12 or 13.

VO: Of course, there was talk of a recovery plan, but the victims of the 10111 failure may never recover.// Beat//

Upsound: "Drive!"
VO: Left stranded by emergency services on the side of the road for 40 minutes, Anastasia had no choice but to call her sister and get her husband to a hospital.

Anastasia: And I was just saying to him just try to stay awake.
//Beat//

Anastasia: And then they came up to me and they said sorry, ma'am. Unfortunately, he's gone. // Beat//
fade to black//

VO: Juan Marcel van Aswegen died that same night.

VO: Dialling 10111 has left Anastasia's family with lifelong trauma.

Anastasia: That's the last number you phone. I am living proof that I was not helped.

VO: Katlego still feels unsafe from her brother and unprotected by a system that may fail her again.

Katlego: I will never in my life use my battery life to call the South African police

VO: The man hit by the car swerving in front of her… was her husband (Over these shots coming up you can put the time and location 7 pm - Sandton, Gauteng) Anastasia: And I started phoning. // I called about 30 times. (screenshots of her phone) VO: Anastasia was calling 10111, the number most South Africans rely on in case of an emergency. Anastasia: if you saw the screenshots on my phone it was on 1% - it was dying. Claude: How many of the 7 million calls could be people,` the most vulnerable in our society that needs assistance, that could be involved in an accident that could save somebody's life? VO: The Public Servants Association National Manager is Claude Naicker. He’s seen the crisis escalate since a 2016 strike by its union members employed at 10111 - demanding better pay and working conditions. Claude: Currently, if you look at Gauteng, we are operating at 74 employees. So what happens to 74 employees that have to man these voluminous calls, they eventually get burned out. During December, which is a peak period. On one shift, there were only 12 employees manning these calls VO: The backlog becomes impossible to manage and the casualties are those whose calls go unanswered. distant ringing tone Anastasia: in those 30 times someone did answer a few times.// CT: Emergency hello?/ VO: The 10111 operator seemed more concernedabout giving Anastasia a reference number. Anastasia: And just no one was coming. Fade to black. VO: In fear of losing his job, John confesses that it's impossible for the scant staff complement of 11 or so people, to handle up toten thousand calls a day.// And what's worse is that some of the radio workstations are broken - a picture of systemic negligence. John: The call taker will take your complaint to the call dispatcher. Derek: But Shouldn't she have realized that you needed an ambulance more than the police? Katlego: And I assumed that all then the police are the ones who must then take me to the hospital or a clinic. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Emergency 10111! With 7 million dropped calls, SA’s most important number isn’t doing its job. Just how dysfunctional are the call centres and how devastating are the effects down the line?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa’s most dialed emergency number SAPS’s 10111 is only operating at 40% capacity. Provincial call centres are understaffed, the employees overworked, underpaid and in some cases working in squalid conditions under tough working practices. We get the inside track from two 10111 operators – one in Gauteng, the other in Durban – exposing the root causes of SA’s crisis in emergency service delivery. And what of the callers in distress, for whom this crisis is a matter of life and death? Where do victims of crime, rape and distress turn to when there is no one on the other end of the line? Even if the calls were answered timeously and efficiently what capacity does the Police Service have to respond to the emergency? Through personal stories and an inside look into how an efficient call centre works, we lay bare the flaws in the police value chain and the impact it has on South Africans who are in desperate need of protection living in one of the most violent and dangerous countries in the world.
metadata.Summary: If you call 10111 in an emergency the likelihood is you won’t get the assistance you need in the timeframe you require it, or you may not be assisted at all. These are the findings from a parliamentary question answered by Police Minister Bheki Cele. I have tracked down two whistleblowers who are prepared to expose their working hell. Both wish to hide their identity but we can get footage of their working environments, one in Durban, the other in midrand – and they will tell their side of the real story behind the devastating government statistics which prove the failure 10111 is, for South Africans when they’re in urgent need of help. Anastasia will never know if her husband’s life might have been saved if there was someone on the other end of the line. Katlego has lost faith in the police, because even though her call was answered by 10111 after being strangled by her brother, when a vehicle was dispatched to help her she was neglected and mistreated by the police, no emergency vehicle was even sent to get her to a hospital. Ash was facing a drunk, aggressive and violent boyfriend when she frantically called 10111. After no response she called the local police station. Luckily they answered but what happened next, makes the response call almost laughable. We speak to people who have become casualties of the 10111 crisis and look at how, even if the number was working at full efficiency, policing down the line may be inadequate to deal with responses effectively. We get an inside look into how an optimal call centre should operate and what is needed to get the assistance required by victims of crime or medical emergency. So the call by the Minister of Police for more recruits to man the centres may not be a solution. Is there a private public partnership and technology that can be a game changer to protecting lives? But at what cost and who will foot the bill in the end?
metadata.Further information: On 3rd January 2023, in response to a parliamentary question by DA Shadow Minister of Police Andrew Whitfield, the following shocking statistics were revealed by Minister of Police Bheki Cele: Only about 40% of required call centre staff were employed across SA. The 10111 number requires police response and more than 7 million calls were dropped. Only 40% of calls were answered. Three provinces. Limpopo, Free State and Northern Cape were unable to give any feedback for the period requested - 2020/21 and 2021/22 to present. The crisis is so severe, that during December when it was required for 126 staff to be working, there were only 12. Many staff members were absent and unable to attend work as they were overworked and could not handle the pressure, according to Claude Naicker, National Manager PSA. The PSA have requested an urgent turnaround plan from Gen. Fani Masimola, within 30 days. But already there is misleading information from the Ministry of Police saying that they have recruited 10 000 new members, but none of these are destined for the call centres according to Naicker, and furthermore, the staff manning the lines has to be trained to be able to deal with the emergencies. This week the Ministry announced they were recruiting more people to man the centres. The question is, is there police capacity to respond on the ground and how long will it take to train and get these members trained and up to speed? In our story on Grade 4 Rape Education, we witnessed first-hand how the 10111 number remained unanswered despite a number of attempts and how the call was dropped. The problem with the emergency number of 10111 goes much deeper. The DA have done further research and randomly called police stations directly and the results were horrific. They are willing to share that report with me. Bobby Stevenson, Shadow MEC for Community Safety highlighted one of the most affected areas, Nelson Mandela Bay. And if one were to use it as a case study for what happens in the police value chain, from call to response, we are made even more acutely aware that South Africans are left unprotected. In his report on the 24th of October 2022, Stevenson highlights the following. In the Nelson Mandela Bay area, absenteeism, severe staff shortages and load shedding had damaged the area’s call centre infrastructure and crippled the call centre. The failure to answer calls is potentially life-threatening. In response to his parliamentary question MEC Xolile Nqatha revealed that even though they had 24 lines only 2 or 3 were operational. Because of load shedding it’s taking up to 45 minutes for the phone lines to come back on. Load shedding destroyed the UPS in September which will cost R4 million to replace, so now the Command and Control Centre System is off line which means that complaints have to be taken manually with no reference numbers. Our two case studies who work in the call centres will reveal recent conditions and confirm the under equipped environments and under staffing they experience. In Durban we will get cell phone footage and in Gauteng I aim to get undercover footage myself, in co-operation with our sources. The frightening thing about all of this, is that even if the call centres were operating optimally could the police respond effectively to those emergencies? MEC Nqatha said that if stations have only two vehicles to attend to an emergency, they can’t proceed to the next emergency until they have completed their investigation, and some stations only have one vehicle. So what does this all mean for the safety and security of South Africans? Who can we rely on in an emergency? And what happens to the people who are in rural areas when there isn’t even someone at the end of a line? Those people are left defenseless. But even in the heart of an urban environment citizens are left to fend for themselves. In October 2020, Anastasia Golfinopoulou saw her husband for the last time alive, as he decided to go for a walk to the local petrol station in the northern suburbs. She decided to pack the kids in the car and go and pick him up. As she was driving down the road a car swerved in front of her and drove up the pavement. Next thing she realises it has hit someone. She jumps out the car with the driver of the vehicle that swerved and sees that he has driven over her husband who was walking home. His almost lifeless body bleeding onto the pavement. Shocked and panicked she starts calling 10111 repeatedly with no response. The other driver does the same. She even calls ER24 still no response. Finally she calls her sister who rushes over to the accident. Forty minutes go by and no one comes. They make the difficult decision to lift him off the ground and get him to a hospital. When they get to Fourways Life, he is pronounced dead a few minutes later. Anastasia has screen shots of her unanswered call logs. Even her sister tried and did not get through. Two years later she still doesn’t know who the driver of the vehicle was and the police say that her file was mixed up with someone elses. When she asks for the investigating officer she is told that he is no longer there. Anastasia is prepared to wear spy glasses and go into the police station to ask for the follow up on her case.
